title: Schroeder's Conjecture
statement_text: If $G$ is a graph of genus $g$, then $c(G) \leq g + 3$.
context_text: Schroeder conjectured in 2001 that the cop number of any genus-$g$ graph is at most $g+3$, meaning one additional cop per handle beyond the planar bound of 3. The conjecture holds for $g=0$ (planar, by Theorem 1) and $g=1$ (toroidal), but remains open for all $g \geq 3$.
paper_contribution: This survey reviews all progress toward Schroeder's conjecture, including the upper bounds $c(G) \leq \lfloor 3g/2 \rfloor + 3$ (Schroeder) and the improvement $c(G) \leq \lfloor 4g/3 \rfloor + D$ (Bowler, Erde, Lehner, Pitz), confirms the conjecture for $g=0$ and $g=1$, and discusses capture time implications.

title: Andreae-Schroeder Conjecture
statement_text: Any toroidal graph has cop number at most $3$.
context_text: Andreae first asked whether toroidal graphs have cop number at most 3; this problem was referenced in Schroeder's paper. No example of a toroidal graph with cop number 4 is known, while the best known upper bound from Schroeder's theorem yields cop number at most 4 for toroidal graphs.
paper_contribution: The survey presents this as an open conjecture and notes that no counterexample is known; the best current upper bound gives cop number at most 4 for toroidal graphs.

title: Clarke-Fiorini-Joret-Theis Conjecture
statement_text: If $g$ is a positive integer, then $\tilde{c}(g) = c(\lfloor g/2 \rfloor)$.
context_text: Clarke, Fiorini, Joret, and Theis conjectured that the lower bound in their Theorem 14 is always tight, relating the maximum cop number $\tilde{c}(g)$ over all non-orientable genus $g$ graphs to the maximum cop number $c(\lfloor g/2 \rfloor)$ over orientable genus $\lfloor g/2 \rfloor$ graphs.
paper_contribution: The survey presents this conjecture alongside Theorem 14, which establishes $c(\lfloor g/2 \rfloor) \leq \tilde{c}(g) \leq \frac{3}{2}(g+1)$.

title: Smallest 3-cop-win planar graph conjecture
statement_text: The smallest order $3$-cop-win planar graph is the dodecahedron.
context_text: It has been proved that the smallest order 3-cop-win graph overall is the Petersen graph. It is conjectured that the smallest planar graph with cop number 3 is the dodecahedron, but this remains open.

title: Classification of planar graphs by cop number
statement_text: Classify which planar graphs have cop number $i$, for $1 \leq i \leq 3$.
context_text: In the game of Cops and Robbers on a (connected) graph $G$, a set of cops and then a robber choose initial vertices; in each round every cop moves to a neighbouring vertex or stays, and then the robber does the same, with perfect information; the cops win if one of them eventually occupies the robber's vertex (capture). The cop number $c(G)$ is the minimum number of cops that guarantees capture; $G$ is $k$-cop-win if $c(G)=k$, and cop-win if $c(G)=1$. Aigner and Fromme proved that every planar graph has cop number at most 3 (using the fact that one cop can guard an isometric path), so every connected planar graph has cop number 1, 2 or 3; the Petersen graph is 3-cop-win and it is conjectured (Baird et al.) that the smallest 3-cop-win planar graph is the dodecahedron, on 20 vertices. Cop-win graphs are precisely the dismantlable graphs (Nowakowski–Winkler, Quilliot), i.e. those whose vertices can be deleted one at a time so that each deleted vertex $u$ has a neighbour $v$ in the remaining graph with $N[u]\subseteq N[v]$; this characterization may eventually help to classify planar cop-win graphs, but the classification of planar graphs with cop number $i$, for $1\le i\le3$, remains open.

title: Classification of outerplanar graphs by cop number
statement_text: Classify which outerplanar graphs are $1$-cop-win and which are $2$-cop-win.
context_text: In the game of Cops and Robbers on a (connected) graph $G$, a set of cops and then a robber choose initial vertices; in each round every cop moves to a neighbouring vertex or stays, and then the robber does the same, with perfect information; the cops win if one of them eventually occupies the robber's vertex (capture). The cop number $c(G)$ is the minimum number of cops that guarantees capture; $G$ is $k$-cop-win if $c(G)=k$, and cop-win if $c(G)=1$. A graph is outerplanar if it can be embedded in the plane with all vertices on the outer face, equivalently if it has no $K_4$ or $K_{2,3}$ minor. Clarke proved that every outerplanar graph has cop number at most 2 (in the 2-connected case the outer face is a Hamilton cycle along which two cops successively enlarge their territory). Cop-win graphs are exactly the dismantlable graphs (vertices can be deleted one at a time, each deleted vertex $u$ having a remaining neighbour $v$ with $N[u]\subseteq N[v]$), but no specific classification of the outerplanar graphs with cop number 1 versus 2 is known; the smallest outerplanar graph with cop number 2 is the 4-cycle.

title: Tightness of linear capture time bound for planar graphs
statement_text: Is the bound $\mathrm{capt}_3(G) \leq 2n$ tight for planar graphs of order $n$? Does there exist a planar graph $G$ of order $n$ with $\mathrm{capt}(G) > n$?
context_text: In the game of Cops and Robbers on a (connected) graph $G$, a set of cops and then a robber choose initial vertices; in each round every cop moves to a neighbouring vertex or stays, and then the robber does the same, with perfect information; the cops win if one of them eventually occupies the robber's vertex (capture). The cop number $c(G)$ is the minimum number of cops that guarantees capture; $G$ is $k$-cop-win if $c(G)=k$, and cop-win if $c(G)=1$. For $k\ge c(G)$, the $k$-capture time $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)$ is the number of rounds (not counting the initial placement) of an optimal play with $k$ cops, i.e. the minimum over cop strategies of the maximum over robber strategies of the length of the game, and $\mathrm{capt}(G)=\mathrm{capt}_{c(G)}(G)$ is the capture time. Every planar graph has cop number at most 3 (Aigner and Fromme). For planar graphs of order $n$, it was first shown that $\mathrm{capt}_3(G)\le(\mathrm{diam}(G)+1)n=O(n^2)$, improving the general bound $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)\le n^{c(G)+1}$ for $k\ge c(G)$, and then the linear bound $\mathrm{capt}_3(G)\le2n$. For cop-win graphs of order $n\ge7$, $\mathrm{capt}(G)\le n-4$, which is attained by planar examples, while in general there are graphs with cop number $k$ and $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)=\Theta(n^{c(G)+1})$ (Kinnersley; Brandt et al.). It is unknown whether the linear bound is tight, and even an example of a planar graph with $\mathrm{capt}(G)>n$ is open at the time of the survey; the survey also asks for tight bounds on the capture time of planar graphs with cop number 2 and 3.

title: Capture time bounds for higher genus graphs
statement_text: What are good bounds on the capture time of graphs of higher genus? (If Schroeder's conjecture holds and $\gamma(G) = g$, then one would have $\mathrm{capt}_k(G) = O(n^{g+4})$ for every $k \geq g+3$.)
context_text: In the game of Cops and Robbers on a (connected) graph $G$, a set of cops and then a robber choose initial vertices; in each round every cop moves to a neighbouring vertex or stays, and then the robber does the same, with perfect information; the cops win if one of them eventually occupies the robber's vertex (capture). The cop number $c(G)$ is the minimum number of cops that guarantees capture; $G$ is $k$-cop-win if $c(G)=k$, and cop-win if $c(G)=1$. For $k\ge c(G)$, the $k$-capture time $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)$ is the number of rounds (not counting the initial placement) of an optimal play with $k$ cops, i.e. the minimum over cop strategies of the maximum over robber strategies of the length of the game, and $\mathrm{capt}(G)=\mathrm{capt}_{c(G)}(G)$ is the capture time. The genus $\gamma(G)$ of $G$ is the minimum genus of an orientable surface on which $G$ embeds, and $n$ is the number of vertices. Schroeder's conjecture states that a graph of genus $g$ has cop number at most $g+3$; it holds for planar and toroidal graphs, and known general bounds are $c(G)\le\lfloor3g/2\rfloor+3$ (Schroeder) and $c(G)\le\lfloor4g/3\rfloor+D$ (Bowler, Erde, Lehner, Pitz). Since $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)\le n^{c(G)+1}$ whenever $k\ge c(G)$ (Berarducci and Intrigila), Schroeder's conjecture would immediately give $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)=O(n^{g+4})$ for every $k\ge g+3$. For planar graphs it is known that $\mathrm{capt}_3(G)\le2n$, and for many cops ($k\ge(19+66\sqrt g)\sqrt n$) one has $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)\le6r(G)\log n$, where $r(G)$ is the radius. The survey raises the examination of capture-time bounds for higher genus graphs as an interesting open question.
